utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam and good afternoon to you. Appearances -- sorry, Mr. Oric, before we proceed any further, I would like to hear from your own mouth that you are receiving interpretation in a language which you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I am receiving interpretation and I can fully follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. You may sit down and good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution. With me today is co-counsel, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Madam Sellers, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam and good afternoon to you and your team. Ms. Richardson, have you discussed with Madam Vidovic how time she's prepared to allow you to take from her own time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. In fact, the Defence has agreed to allow me 15 minutes of their time which I appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very generous on their part. They are more generous than I am. I would have allowed you six to seven minutes. Yes, any preliminaries? None?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring the witness in, please. Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, today during the cross-examination, I ask leave to sit because I still have health problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic, you don't need to ask me each time. Take it that you have my permission or otherwise you have our permission to do that, to remain seated until you are in a position where you can stand. It's up to you when the time comes for that. Just let us know. Otherwise you don't need to ask us each time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Omerovic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you are receiving interpretation, so if there is a problem, let me know like you did yesterday. I suggest you take your seat. You are still testifying under oath, which you don't need to repeat today, and you are now going to be asked a few questions for the next 15 minutes by Ms. Richardson and then she will be followed by Madam Vidovic with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omerovic. Yesterday at the end of the Court session, you advised the Trial Chamber that there were lawyers in Srebrenica, excuse me, and I showed you a document with a list of lawyers. I would ask you today, in addition to the list we saw which included Avdo Majstorovic, could you tell us whether there was another lawyer in Srebrenica that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the people on the list, there was no other lawyer who had graduated from university in Srebrenica at that point in time. One person from the list, Esad Nukic, was in Tuzla at that time because he had duties assigned to him by the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, or, rather, the Transitionary Municipal Council which had then been established as the legislative organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to that, he had been in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had been the secretary first of the War Presidency and then of the Transitional Municipal Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with Amir Mehmedovic? I may not be pronouncing it properly.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that name. I have never heard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if I show you the document with his name on it, you can tell us if you're familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have P539 shown to the witness. It is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you look at the person who wrote this letter, the assistant to the commander for legal affairs, Amir Mehmedovic, could you tell us if you're familiar with there individual?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Mehmedovic. You mispronounced it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember what this person looked like. I might be able to remember him better if I heard his nickname, but I'm sure that he had not graduated from law school. I might have performed these duties, but he was certainly not a lawyer who had graduated from university. He had some other sort of education. I'm sure that I knew all the lawyers in Srebrenica who had graduated as lawyers and I knew all their names and all of them had been assigned to various duties and positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to another area. Thank you, Madam Usher that's all I have with respect to that document. You testified yesterday that you attended the War Presidency meetings, in particular one on November 9th, 1992. Could you tell us if you attended other meetings of the War Presidency as well?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps two others. I'm sure about one. There were two or three meetings of the War Presidency altogether that I attended. One was when we discussed the organisation of the court and the problem of the lower court and the problems of public law and order, crime, murders and so on. And there was another meeting a few months before the fall of Srebrenica. This was perhaps in March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was Naser Oric present at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present at the last of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Srebrenica, how often in addition to the meetings, did you come in contact with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did he live in the same vicinity as you did?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation, he would sometimes frequent a flat, visit a flat, which was in the building I resided in. There was some young men living in that flat, and after the demilitarisation, he would visit there. In 1992 and 1993, I saw him on one or two occasions entering the building I resided in, in 1992 and 1993. And in 1994 he would come more off.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: During the times you saw Naser Oric when you were in Srebrenica, could you tell us what his appearance was? In other words, was he clean shaven or did he wear a beard, any facial hair?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had short hair. He always cut his hair short. And he had a small beard, some growth on his chin, a long time has elapsed. It's hard to remember. But I would like to add that in Srebrenica there was a person who resembled Naser Oric physically. This was Hazim Omerovic from the village of Voljavica near Bratunac who resided in Srebrenica all the time, and he looked a lot like Naser Oric and he had a similar hairstyle and people who didn't know Naser well might confuse the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Ms. Richardson. One moment, Ms. Richardson. You described Naser Oric for us. The question actually related to the period that you would see him in Srebrenica, and I understood that to be 1992, 1993, 1994. Was it always the same appearance throughout these three years or did it change from time to time? For example, did you ever see him with long hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never wore long hair in Srebrenica, or at least I didn't see that he had longer hair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him clean shaven and not with a small beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably did, but those are details it's hard to recall after all those years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate that. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that you -- the Court contacted Tuzla by means of communication system that was coded. You also testified about couriers. Did yourself or anyone else in the court contact Tuzla by any other means?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two contacts with Tuzla through a ham radio station. When we had problems in extending detention for some persons who were listed as members of the army and we could not extend their custody and the time had come for their release, I tried to contact the president of the district military court in Tuzla. From the president of the War Presidency in Srebrenica, I received approval to use a ham radio station to talk to Tuzla. This conversation was scheduled but instead of the president of the district military court, Mr. Hajrudin Halilovic, who was a judge of that court spoke to me. Until the war he had been the president of the lower court in Srebrenica. I wanted to ask them to send us as soon as possible either a decision on the extension of custody or the termination of custody for the persons we were holding in detention because we had no legal basis to keep them in detention any longer. But he told me we could not discuss these matters over that communication -- method of communication because it was easy to listen into.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, Mr. Omerovic. We only have but so much time. Where was this ham radio station located?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was located in the post office building in Srebrenica, and the other was located behind the municipal building in a -- in a room that was very shabby and small, and three ham radio operators changed shifts there, and all the citizens who wanted to communicate with their families elsewhere would come there and try to establish communication with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like the photograph to be shown to the exhibit -- excuse me, to the witness, and that is Exhibit 523 and it is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again if you have got more important questions I would suggest you move to those rather than to stick with this, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would only take less than a minute and I am keeping an eye on my 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. A minute over 15 minutes is quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is this the type of radio that you used to contact Tuzla? If you could just answer with a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or no.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less it looked like this. It had these buttons and the thing you hod to speak into. So it looked approximately like this. I can't be sure it's identical but it did look like this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any other questions with respect to that document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, did you in your capacity as the president of the court during the time that were you in Srebrenica receive any reports of war crimes such as destruction of property or maltreatment of prisoners or any reports regarding the death of prisoners, from anyone including the military police or Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had absolutely no information of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports from the Prosecutor of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one additional photograph to be shown to the witness and that is from P419. ERN number 03617726, and this is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I really don't have any more time, Mr. Omerovic, so if you could just tell us briefly if you recognise this picture and what is it? What building is it?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the building of the police station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's 03617726. The next is 03617720.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same building. It's the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you and then 03617716.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the municipal building of Vogosca municipality and next to it is the building adjacent to it, actually. It's the building of the lower court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have an office in this building at any time during your time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993, we had first one office when I was on my own, and then two. It was in this building upstairs because at that time, in the billing of the Court, refugees were accommodated. So we had first one office and then two, and these were in the municipal building upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The next photograph 03617714.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would just note that we have exceeded the 15 minute limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This is my last one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have exceeded it by a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wouldn't want my learned friend to trespass on our good nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This is my -- this is the last photograph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is the building of the lower court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were any other offices in this building -- were there any other offices in this building?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground floor, after the establishment of the municipal prison, the prison was located on the ground floor. The court was upstairs on the second floor and refugees were still accommodated on the first floor, so we were on the second floor. Refugees were in between on the first floor. And the prison was downstairs on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omerovic. I would like to put a number of questions to you that can be answered very briefly, either with a "yes" if you agree with what I put to you or with a "no" if you don't agree since our time is limited. Besides this, when I finish my question, please make a short pause before you begin to answer for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you. Mr. Omerovic, Bratunac municipality before the war had about 33.619 inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 21.535 Muslims lived there which amounted to 64.2 per cent, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in 1992, there were almost twice as many Muslims in Bratunac as there were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of this, or regardless of the fact that the Muslim population was in the absolute majority in early 1992, within the scope of the conception of dividing municipalities, the Serbian Democratic Party joined these municipalities into the Birac autonomous region. I'm referring to Bratunac and Srebrenica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In late 1991, and early 1992, the JNA located heavy weapons in various localities in Ljubovija and pointed the barrels towards the Muslim neighbourhoods in Bratunac, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The military training of local Serbs, starting in March 1992 in the Bratunac area, was carried out publicly, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1991 and 1992, the Serb nationalist propaganda reached its peak?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what they said was that Serbs were under threat in Srebrenica and that they would be safe only if they remained within a greater Serbia, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This appeared in the Belgrade newspapers, on television shows, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the town of Bratunac itself, slogans appeared such as, "This is Serbia," "Move out Turks before you've been slaughtered." Large knives were drawn in these graffiti, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, contrary to the Serb propaganda, it was, in fact, the Muslims who were in danger in that area?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Starting in March 1992, and onwards, it was their property that was destroyed in Bratunac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were numerous incidents in which Muslims were intimidated?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Starting in 1991, as of September, these incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In early April 1992, the Serbs in Bratunac and the villages around Bratunac were armed, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As soon -- as early as the 10th of April 1992, in the Bratunac area, you saw people wearing camouflage uniforms with insignia saying "SAO" armed with automatic weapons, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. In the centre of Bratunac I saw people in camouflage uniforms carrying -- wearing SAO insignia and these were people who had a murky past.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This SAO insignia means Serbian autonomous region, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Men -- the men in uniform, which you have just described, were local Serbs whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among the Muslims, there was panic, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. They all fled the towns to the surrounding Muslim villages where they hid.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is why you yourself decided to leave Bratunac with your family, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. The moment I learned that the Serbs had set up checkpoints at all exits from the town, which they were guarding with weapons, I decided to leave while I still had the chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Many Muslims who remained in Bratunac were arrested and there was mass murder of Muslims, am I right in saying that more than 2.000 Muslims in Bratunac were killed during the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a large number of people were killed and there is information to this effect, their names are known. Mass executions were carried out and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the village of Bibici which you mentioned in your testimony, you were stopped by armed soldiers and they were in camouflage uniforms, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When on the 10th or 11th I left Srebrenica for the village of Krusev Do, in the village of Bibici there was a patrol in camouflage uniform standing in front of my car and they had balaclava helmets on their heads, with slits for the eyes. One was wearing the uniform of a reserve policeman, and two of them had these masks. I was with my wife and child.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was did they wear camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the area of Podravanje you were stopped by the local Serbs, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They too did have uniforms and automatic weapons, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had parade JNA uniforms or the so-called combat fatigues. They had automatic weapons, they had Motorolas and they were in groups of about a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the village of Podravanje, they had two checkpoints, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Muslim villages surrounding Srebrenica and Bratunac, as of April 1992, there was shortage of food and medication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw that yourself in Krusev Do and Luka?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people were short of food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason for that was because the movement of Muslims even then was limited by the set up checkpoints set up by the Serbs, as well as the armed forces that were deployed in various villages, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One couldn't move too much and go and buy food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As of late April, Serb forces started shelling Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Serb planes participated in those attacks as of June and July 1992, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. They dropped bombs on Luka and Krusev Do where I stayed with my wife and child and they dropped cassette bombs, cluster bombs, and these villages were exclusively populated by civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Cluster bombs are very destructive and in particular against civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Local Serbs attacked and killed from ambush and they would kill civilians, Muslims, entire families in June and July 1992 were killed in that way in the area of Bratunac, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I can even describe some of the incidents, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was particularly pronounced in the area towards Zajnovo [phoen] or Abdulici because there is the same village with two names as well as Voljevica, Zaluzje [phoen] and towards Glogova but elsewhere as well, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in all of the above.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Krusev Do that you spoke about, as well as many other villages, were completely isolated because in between them, there were Serbian army strong holds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. They were completely surrounded without any sort of communication with the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the reason for the situation in Krusev Do. It was very grave without food and medication, and you had to leave the place?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no food, medication, physicians, electricity, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival to Srebrenica in mid-July 1992, you found a very serious situation there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a desperate one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to that period, there were Serbs there, the city was devastated and there was no electricity, medication, or food there either?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Life was actually paralysed, blocked?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally had to ask for food from the people you knew in order to survive?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't have much for themselves either.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You risked your life going to the nearby Muslim villages to get anything to eat for your family?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even once I went as far down as to the area of Bratunac to the village of Voljavica between the Chetnik positions during the night in order to bring some food, but I wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would happen on occasion that for days you had nothing to eat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once Mr. Majstorovic said that you looked very poorly, you were in a bad shape, and he gave you a bag of nuts, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Majstorovic's brother, who was my colleague and attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For a while, you survived eating a nut a day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would take that nut to my work, when I started working with the court, and perhaps around 11 or noon, I would eat it and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, you saw some old women starving to death and you gave one of them their nut, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a Catholic woman, a Croat, who fled from Rogatica to Zepa and from Zepa to Srebrenica because she had no place to stay in Zepa, and she was there together with two other elderly women. She came to the municipal building and the president of the War Presidency would on occasion give them a coupon so that they could get a meal from the local kitchen while there was food, and they were very exhausted. She was shivering, she was close to 80. I took out that nut and gave it to her and she ate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So on that day, you had nothing to eat?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was early fall 1992?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People, elderly people, children, women, began dying from hunger and diseases?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe those women that we talked about died from hunger and because of the winter that was coming, because I never saw them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Children, in particular, suffered from hunger. They went around town on a daily basis going from one door to the next begging for food?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. Every day between 10 to 15 children would knock on one's door, asking for a piece of bread. They were pale, exhausted and in very poor shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Falls in eastern Bosnia are quite cold but winters are terrible?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Winters are very heavy with lots of snow, very cold.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the temperatures go as low as minus 30 degrees Centigrade?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Death was a daily occurrence, there was shelling, bombs dropping from planes, and the situation was very terrible in Srebrenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were bombed on a daily basis. The centre of Srebrenica was attacked by planes every day and there was constant shelling, particularly from multiple rocket launchers and they would simply drop around 30 to 40 shells in the area of the town at once. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the town was in total chaos -- total state of chaos, some people went wild?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some people did go wild and some women as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By the end of 1992, it looked like Srebrenica would fall?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no possibility to defend, no ammunition, no food, no medication.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It seemed that tens of thousands of people who were in Srebrenica were facing death from hunger and cold?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how I saw it, that all of those people will die, collectively, en masse.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Terrible hunger, death, and siege had to be stopped, had it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were looking desperately for a way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People had to start or go into action to get some food in order to feed their loved ones?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could either die, starve to death, or we could get killed trying to get food. Otherwise we would die any way so we had to go and search for food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to ask you about, Mr. Omerovic. You were there, you are a person who can assess a given situation. Had those people not gone into actions in Serbian villages, thousands of people would have died because of the siege?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no food in Srebrenica whatsoever. All of those people would have died. We had nothing to use as food. There was no humanitarian aid. We were absolutely under siege and no one was trying to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The weaponry that was seized from the Serb villages meant that their families were able to survive because the fight for the food and survival could continue?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a bit of a delayed reaction but I believe the witness is testifying to -- the people would have starved, et cetera. Perhaps we can just be a little bit more specific about what people, what areas he's referring to. Are we talking about Srebrenica, the areas outside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I that took it he's talking about Srebrenica. However if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There's -- there has been other testimony about different villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Omerovic, you've heard Ms. Richardson. If you can expand on that, if you're talking only about Srebrenica because that's what you know, then you stick to Srebrenica. If you are also familiar with the situation as it obtained in nearby villages or in other areas, provided you know this yourself, then you can of course amplify on what you've told us already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire area of Srebrenica was exposed to hunger because in all of the villages, there were lots of refugees. So the villages plus the urban part of the settlement, all of the people there were hungry. There was no food whatsoever. Perhaps someone could harvest a bit but in each village there was a lot of refugees, not only in the town, so everyone was hungry. And in the area of Srebrenica, the soil is not very favourable to grow wheat and so on. So there was no food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Omerovic. So people had two options, attack and take weapons and food or die; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. There was no other way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even yourself, who were a judge at the time, were one of those people because you were trying desperately to get food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to take that step. I had my wife and my child who was four. We had nothing to eat. I was forced to either die or get some food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, it is correct, is it not, that the army did not organise civilians including yourself to follow them into action?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each person on their own went trying to get some food for themselves and families. Entire families went, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the armed forces did not organise you to join them in their actions and operations?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went to the area of Bjelovac, Loznica Rijeka, and Sase because you found about the forthcoming action?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that there would be an attack was something that wasn't possible to be kept secret because people who were armed, the combatants, did not live in barracks, they lived with their families?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. They lived with their wives and children. They would stand guard so everyone knew when the next operation would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They would talk about that in their houses and the word would get Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. around?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Srebrenica is a small area, very small area, that was still free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Before you put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do apologise. With respect to the witness just gave an answer about "they." What's -- sorry, they lived with their wives and children and the reference to "they," I would only ask that he be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond, our colleagues from the Prosecution can clarify this objection if their redirect. I did previously mention combatants in my question and the witness understood me perfectly. He meant combatants lived in their houses and not in the barracks, and he understood me and I see no reason for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you. I agree entirely with you because he uses the word "combatants" and that's taken to be fighters so that's what the witness must have been referring to, so let's try to interrupt as little as we can, please, and move ahead. Yes, Ms. Vidovic. You were about to put another question, a new question, to the witness. I'm sorry for the interruption, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So combatants could not prevent thousands of starving civilians to join them because those people sometimes were without food for days and they couldn't stop them from joining them?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police could not have done that, nor anyone else, could they?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there were operations to find food, everyone was trying to get food. That was the only opportunity to get some.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went to the area of Bjelovac around the 14th or the 15th of December 1992, as you stated yesterday. You also stated that you were unable to enter those villages because the shelling started. In other words, those villages of Loznica Rijeka Bjelovac, Loznica, and Sase were shelled at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got as far as the village of Podloznik. That was a Muslim village that was in the free territory of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic --

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't reach the villages because the shells already began landing and one could hear the planes shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, could you help us out here? How far is Podloznik from Bjelovac and Sase, and Loznica Rijeka, in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be at least four to five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The area was shelled by the Serbs, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And still even though there was shelling, lots of civilians went there, including women and children, and there were lines a few kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long, uninterrupted column of the elderly, women, children who were as young as ten, and it was already December. It was winter. There was no food, and everyone went down there, irrespective of the shooting but I didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were desperate people, ready to kill for food, ready to kill each other poor food, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When describing the situation in Srebrenica in late 1992, and early 1993, in your previous testimony, I will quote paragraph 34 of your statement, you remember that you signed this statement. I will quote paragraph 34 and you said, "Every day it was said that Srebrenica was going to fall. I did not address anybody about the lack of work in the period from October 1992 to May 1993. It was on account of the terrible humanitarian situation and that nothing was working in Srebrenica. The surrounding villages were falling under Serb control one after the other. The refugees had filled the whole of Srebrenica. The working of the court was not a priority at that time. The town was dying and it was not possible to pay attention to such things." Mr. Omerovic, does what you said here reflect the real reasons for the complete impossibility of the work of the court and the impossibility of any kind of productive work at the time?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that situation, nothing could function properly. No organs, nothing, could function. The situation was desperate. It was disastrous.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the daily struggle to survive, people weren't interested in anything else?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were interested only in how to survive. Everything else was unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The authorities in Srebrenica were not functioning for this reason, and not because someone in Srebrenica did not want the government authorities to function properly, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. Under such conditions, it's impossible to secure the normal functioning of government bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even so, the War Presidency tried to set up some kind of court?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo Tursunovic himself wanted that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, you described a person who you said was the military police commander. In your previous statement, when you mentioned the military police, I will quote paragraph 59 of your statement, you said the following: "Its composition, level of equipment necessary knowledge, education level of the staff, did not allow them to run a procedure or to submit a report. I do not think they did anything regarding public security. That job was done by the civilian police." And in connection with this, I will ask you the following: In practice, in Srebrenica at that time, it was thought that it was the job of the civilian police to initiate proceedings against perpetrators of misdemeanours and crimes or anything to do with public security; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that the military police had no equipment, that for the most part these people had no weapons?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, weapons had to be at the front lines because of the terrible pressure of the Serb forces throughout this time from the beginning of the war in 1992 until the demilitarisation in 1993. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Srebrenica itself, you couldn't even recognise the police because people had no uniforms, no weapons, and all the uniforms there were kept at the front lines, and the people there changed shifts to defend this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now put some questions to you about demilitarisation. After the demilitarisation, the army existed only formally in Srebrenica, in the Srebrenica area, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify this a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, one of Their Honours asked me about the competency of the secretariat of defence in every municipality, including that of Srebrenica. I don't know whether I explained this sufficiently, but this municipal organ was there to recruit young people for their regular military service, and after their regular military service was over, this organ continued giving them their wartime assignments. In other words, they kept lists of soldiers who could be called up if there was a war. That was the job of the National Secretariat for Defence. And we had a similar situation. All the surrounding villages had fallen except for Potocari and Sutjeska, and only the centre of Srebrenica was left. All the people who had been defending those villages found themselves in the town of Srebrenica. The demilitarisation took place. Every one was now a civilian. There were no soldiers to be seen. Everybody was equal. However in this period after the demilitarisation, somebody again drew up lists, establishing units. This was the job of the Secretariat for National Defence, and I can assert with full responsibility that all these men were civilians and that none of them were armed, that they were all the same. In the court we had problems because of this. We had a civilian before us and there was a list on which he was listed as a soldier. In my view, this was simply a list to be used should there be an attack on Srebrenica and for no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So when I say that the army existed only in formal terms, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The army was not allowed to act in the demilitarised zone in any way. That was illegal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers of international organisations, primarily UNPROFOR, followed and confiscated weapons and prevented any kind of military activity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, all this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the civilian police was the only police authorised to take measures against perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. After the demilitarisation, real civilian police was set up. I think that uniforms were made for them, they had pistols, they had police insignia, and they really began to do their job professionally. You could see that the situation had normalised and that little by little, regular, normal organs were being established, such as exist in any state.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this certainly included the detection of crimes and the discovery of their perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the chaos that you have described, with the thousands of refugees, of whom no records were kept, in the situation of all-prevailing psychosis, you will agree with me that it was very difficult to get any kind of information?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was very difficult for anybody to do any kind of job, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The revulsion people felt towards the Serbs, who represented death to these refugees, was such that to get any kind of information from these people about possible crimes perpetrated against Serbs and their property was almost impossible, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Those would have been unsuccessful attempts. Had anybody tried under those conditions to do that, they would not have succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally never received information that any crime had been committed against Serbs or their property, apart from those that were dealt with in the regular legal procedure and that's how we know about them, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have no reason to think that in Srebrenica any kind of crime was committed by its fighters apart from the court cases that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. We were completely surrounded, condemned to death either by starvation or by being killed, and the people of Srebrenica had to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were shown a criminal report against Emir Halilovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Today you were asked by the Prosecutor about criminal reports again. As the president of the court or as a judge, you could not receive criminal reports. It was the public prosecutor who received them?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The public security station or the police would submit these reports directly to the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A criminal report would reach you only provided the public prosecutor moved you to begin a proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what was provided for by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise, you would never even learn there was a criminal report unless you received a motion to begin an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only after the public prosecutor submits a motion to start an investigation, then the criminal report is attached to the motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the motion to initiate an investigation was submitted only if there was sufficient evidence, prima facie evidence, received by the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was up to the prosecutor make that assessment based on the criminal report and the supporting materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness Exhibit P505? We will look at only one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please look at the page with the large number 03615757? Your Honour, those are pages 3 and 4 in the English version of document P505. This is an addendum to the report of the 31st of October 1995, of the judge of the lower court, Azid [phoen] Akagic, of the 13th of November 1995. Witness, have you found this page?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to save time, I will tell you that this refers to the investigation of a certain crime of murder and the manner of proceeding of the prosecutor. Please look at there and I will quote to you the relevant part which is just -- which is in the lower part of the document and begins with the words, I will quote this part. "After instructions from the Court in Tuzla, the lower court in Srebrenica, in all these cases, declared itself not competent and handed on the cases to the district military court in Tuzla. As of that time, the prosecutor's office of the lower court in Tuzla only registered these cases mentioning that they were to be forwarded to the court in Tuzla. As there were large numbers of these cases, they could not be sent on to the court in Tuzla by computer, especially the sketches and the supporting material, and there were no prerequisites to start investigations. A convenient moment was awaited to forward these cases to the public Prosecutor's office in Tuzla." In connection with this, I will put a question to you. This document shows, does it not, that the lower public prosecutor's office, in cases where it was the district prosecutor's office of the military court in Tuzla that had competence, they only registered these cases, noting that they were to be forwarded to the prosecutor's office in Tuzla. In other words, they only registered the criminal reports in question, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is confirmed by Mrs. Djulzira Akagic. She was only registering these cases and awaiting a convenient moment or rather the possibility of forwarding them on to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. This document also shows that these cases could not be delivered to Tuzla because of the supporting material which could not be sent by computer?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, it's correct, is it not, that these cases never reached you because it was the district military court in Tuzla that had jurisdiction, not your court?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, and I don't even know what cases these are. I'm not familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, then, that the prosecutor could receive reports pertaining to certain crimes that you never heard of, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is also confirmed by this information from the prosecutor. I agree absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put away this document. We don't need it any more. Yesterday and today, when speaking about the military police, you said that the equipment and training of the military police, regardless of whom they were subordinate to, were not such that they were able to collect evidence, check information, and submit criminal reports, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct. There were no professional policemen who had been trained as such and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the demilitarisation, you said that nothing was functioning properly there. The security organ was not functioning properly, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question? I wasn't concentrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about the functioning or non-functioning of the authorities in Srebrenica before the demilitarisation, you said that nothing was working properly there. This included the security organ. Do you -- are you -- do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully. The circumstances were such that nothing could function properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. JUDGE AGIUS: Microphone, please, and start again because the interpreters obviously didn't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to offer, or rather ask a clarification from the witness because the record states that nothing could function properly, but the witness was actually saying that nothing could have functioned in general, as principle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Under such circumstances, nothing could have functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and Mr. Omerovic had actually made this point earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, I wanted to ask you something about military commanders. You mentioned some yesterday. Local military commanders were not educated, were they? These were mainly people chosen by farmers to lead their armed groups and defend their villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely the way of organising and electing commanders. There were not educated or trained. They had no military expertise. These were just regular people who lived in those villages, and amongst themselves the people from the village would choose as commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you knew those people, with the exception of Nedzad Bektic and Mr. Dzananovic, who did possess some prior training, others were not people who had any sort of training or education?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not only in the military sense of the word, but generally speaking, these were people of very low education, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, the commanders were exceptionally poorly educated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them literally were illiterate?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to put a document before the witness, and this is an excerpt from the law on criminal procedure. This is a chapter headed "Criminal report, Article 1448." Mr. Omerovic, you are probably familiar with this piece of legislation. I would kindly ask you to look at it. I will quote para 1 and 3 of Article 148. Para 1 states the following, "It shall be the duty of all state organs, organisations of associated labour and other self managing organisations and communities to report any crimes that are prosecuted ex officio, of which they were informed or of which they learned by any other means." Para 3, "Submitting the report, state organs, organisations of associated labour and other self-managing organisations and communities shall cite any evidence known to them and undertake measures to safeguard any evidence of the crime, any objects with which or with the assistance of which the crime was committed, and any other evidence. Mr. Omerovic, it is correct, is it not, that this article of the law on criminal procedure regulates the duties of all state organs, as well as other organs, to report the criminal offences they have knowledge of, and that they submit evidence that is known to them. In relation to that, simply put, by law a criminal report could have been submitted by any of the aforementioned organs but would you agree with me if I said that in order to submit a criminal report, that that is a separate thing from submitting a report and submitting the evidence corroborating the report?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. All of the aforementioned state organs mentioned in Article 148 are duty bound to submit a criminal report but to secure evidence and the rest that is mentioned is a different thing. Not all of those organs can do such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, any of the organs could submit a report given they knew of the offence, but in order for them to collect evidence, as prescribed by law, that was something that could be done only by the authorised or competent organs?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they needed the minimum equipment and personnel required, the personnel should be trained adequately?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The people to do that should have some training in police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The formation called the armed forces of Srebrenica prior to the demilitarisation, such people were non-existent among theirs ranks?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. And I stated that in my statement given to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good time for a break, unless it is too early, but I will now move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. If it's more convenient for you to stop here, we'll stop here. That's not going to make a difference. So we'll have a 25 minute break starting from now. Basically we'll start again at 4.00 exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the latest document I used, could we please assign it a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, what's the next number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D288, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will become Defence Exhibit D288. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I please ask the usher to put two documents before the witness? These are Prosecutor's exhibits P48, P49, and I would want the witness to see them together and I will, having used those documents, ask for a joint Defence number but for the time being, these are P48 and 49.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document P48 is an alleged document from the headquarters of the armed forces of Srebrenica from the security organ from the 31st of January 1993, attention of Milisav Milovanovic, and P49 is a note in handwriting, also addressed to Milisav Milovanovic. Witness, could you please take a look at the typed document? First and foremost, could you direct your attention to what it states in the upper-right corner? Take a look at the date, that is the 31st of January 1993. Would you agree with me that in the upper right corner, it states, "Court martial Srebrenica to the commission for mediation with the enemy."? Then please take a look at the last sentence of this alleged note. I quote, "He's a person of interest to security but has been examined thoroughly. Therefore, and for the proceedings, he's put at the disposal of the military high court to render the final decision." And in relation to that I wanted to ask you the following: In January and February 1993, and up until the demilitarisation, there was only the misdemeanours court in Srebrenica, and you testified about it, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And this court was never set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was discussed during a Presidency session but it was never set up and it never became operational?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you know, in Srebrenica, there was no such thing as the commission for mediation with the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the existence of such a commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the other document in handwriting? Please take a look at the part of the document above the stamp. It states, "The opinion and proposal to the higher military court." And concerning that I wanted to ask you the following: There was no higher military court this Srebrenica, was it?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it was never set up in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did exist in Tuzla was the district military court?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, within the legal framework of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there never used to be a higher military court. Concerning appeals against decisions of the district military court, that was dealt by the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are, and yesterday we saw that in a document. There was an accused who appealed against a decision on detention by the district military court in Tuzla, and he appealed to the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to these documents, I have the last question. You never saw these documents. You never received them as a misdemeanour judge in January 1993 or at any other time?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw these documents. For the first time I was shown the typed-out document yesterday by the Prosecutor, but I did not know of its existence previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we assign a number to these documents that bear the number of P48 and P49? But I would ask for a joint number, of Defence, unless you believe that could cause problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of causing problems. I don't see the utility for it. They exist there so you have made reference to the two of them, 48, 49, and the transcript shows that you have made reference to them sort of conjointly, even though I don't think that that is the right word, so I don't -- if you want to produce them as Defence exhibits together, I mean, get a photocopy of that and I will give them a Defence number but I honestly don't see the need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It is not necessary, then. We do have a copy. I appreciate your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now ask you something on a different topic. It is correct, Mr. Omerovic, is it not, that the War Presidency of Srebrenica asked for an advice from both Tuzla and Sarajevo in order to know what to do in the given situation when they had no courts at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In such a grave situation, we asked for an opinion of the Ministry of Justice from Sarajevo, and I can offer further explanation. The War Presidency of Srebrenica was not competent to appoint judges of the basic court. It could only appoint judges to the misdemeanours court. But as for the competencies of appointing judges of the lower court, they had none. That's why we asked for an opinion of the Ministry of Justice from Sarajevo and from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They also asked for help to establish those courts?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did send such documents to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Omerovic, it is fully certain, is it not, that before the 25th of May 1993, in Srebrenica, no regulations reached the town, at least the regulation that was put into force in 1992 and 1993, that is the laws that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina until that moment?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And the documents that did arrive -- arrived through the UN via helicopter flight with the draft of the Vance-Owen Plan and some of the regulation also arrived then because we wanted to be updated on the new legislation. We were completely cut off so we had no idea what regulation should be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask the usher to put D209 before the witness. This is a document from the lower court in Srebrenica, number 2/93 of the 10th of December 1993. Mr. Omerovic, you saw this document yesterday. It was shown to you by the Prosecutor. Could you please briefly have a look and then I would ask the following: You told us that the basic court, as well as the basic prosecutor's office in Srebrenica was established in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document is actually a report that you put together as the president of the court for the year of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was forwarded to the district court in Tuzla to advise the president of the situation and our activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now quote the relevant part of paragraph 4 from the page bearing the ERN number 01840661. There you state, "We are unable to put into -- to conduct expert analysis because there are no people qualified in the territory under the competence of this Court. Also, we cannot assign a Defence counsel to represent perpetrators in cases where representation is required because there are no -- also we are not able to provide --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- due to the non-functioning transfer of payments and non-existence of a monetary unit, perpetrators of misdemeanors are sentenced to prison or given reprimands. That is the only way to protect law and in order because before we started operating the situation was chaotic. We received official Gazettes for 1992 and 1993 only in November 1993 and they are in incomplete. Currently, we face problems due to the lack of appropriate forms and paper that could be used for typing. The Court building accommodates refugees and the judicial archives have been destroyed." In relation to that I wanted to ask the following: This document is or represents the real situation in which you were supposed to implement laws; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad that these documents were found, because without them, my testimony would not be as convincing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omerovic. Not only did you not have the required experts for expert analyses, you did not even have appropriate forms or paper for typing on?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We even used old pieces of paper which had already been used on one side, and then we used the other side, which was blank. In 1994, in late 1994, the UN civilian police started providing us with a packet of 500 sheets of paper from time to time, and that was when we had the paper we required. Let me say that because of the lack of regulations, in order to illustrate for the Court the difficulties and problems we faced there, because we did not have the amendments to the laws adopted by Bosnia and Herzegovina after the outbreak of the war, we didn't know that some crimes had been abolished, such as illegal appropriation of state-owned property, and we received about 500 criminal reports for this crime which no longer existed. The police continued to submit criminal reports to us. I have tried to explain what it meant for us not to have the required legislation at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your building was populated by refugees and your court archives were completely destroyed, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The refugees moved into the building because there was absolutely no where for them to stay. They stayed in all the offices. They occupied all the offices. They turned over the furniture and slept on it. They used our paper, our documents, to burn in fires and to warm themselves. And no one was able to prevent this. There was nothing we could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Everything you have described happened in late 1992 up until the demilitarisation in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was in this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The judges appointed to that court in mid-1993, together with you, had no experience as judges. They were unable to consult even the jurisprudence of that court, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We were obliged to appoint the lawyers that were there because we didn't have any others so we didn't have anyone with experience. Of the four judges, I had the most experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Omerovic, in this period, you did not have the basic conditions for work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Everything you did was symbolic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Trials could not take place?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have the conditions to hold a trial, because even the investigative proceedings were incomplete. Since we did not have the possibility of expert analyses, we could not appoint Defence counsel, we did not have the conditions for executing long-term prison sentences. We only had a few cells. We didn't have a prison where people could serve Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prison sentences of several years, longer sentences, for serious crimes such as murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put away this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document P507? This is a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, you saw this document yesterday. This is a criminal report against Emir Halilovic, number KU14/93, the 28th of July 1993. Please look at the page bearing number 03648894, the part that refers to the attachments, would you please clarify something? Please take a look at what it says here, what is enclosed, and this -- there is a forensic report here about an examination of a corpse. Have you found this?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, that medical report on examining a body is not the same thing as an autopsy in our part of the world, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was only an external examination of the body, am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. In Srebrenica, we could only externally examine the body. We did not have the personnel who could do anything else. Zdenko Trilaz [phoen] was the medical expert appointed to the court. 21

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Vidovic, and thank you, Mr. Omerovic, for this explanation. Let's make this clear. I am understanding perfectly well the distinction that you tried to -- to make, so basically what you're referring to is that this would not be an autopsy report or a post-mortem report but it would be what we would call a "levee du corps," correct? In other words, when a body, a dead -- levee du corps. Basically, what I mean is this, that as soon as a person arrives, the body of a dead person has been found, apart from the usual investigators, a doctor, a medical doctor, is called on the scene, and he will look at the body and he will issue a certificate describing the body and on that certificate he will also indicate whether there are external signs of violence to start with and whether the body is dead and how long that body has probably been dead and this sort of thing.
