This is what you are understanding by what is written supposedly in the B/C/S text; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. This should not be translated as autopsy. This is the reason I asked the witness about it. In our language, an autopsy implies that the body was opened up and that it was examined inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, witness?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. An autopsy can determine whether there are internal injuries and what was the exact cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when -- this is where I need the help of the interpreters. I'm going to read the way I know what we have here in B/C/S, and then please translate to me as I go along. [Interpretation] Inspection of the forensic medical finding on an examination of the body of Stojan Krsmanovic. [In English] I think that's clear enough. It should never have appeared as examination of autopsy report of the body of Stojan Krsmanovic because levee du corps is completely -- something ... Anyway, thank you, Madam Vidovic because one would require only the presence of a doctor, who would not necessarily be a pathologist, but for a postmortem you definitely need experienced pathologists, experienced in conducting post-mortem reports. And the report of one is completely different from the report of the other. Yes, Mr. Omerovic, thank you also for explaining this to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the case of Emir Halilovic, Witness, I will ask you the following. The case of Emir Halilovic, who committed the triple murder against citizens of Srebrenica of Serb ethnicity is a specific case because before it was dealt with and before the suspect was arrested and sent to Tuzla, help and assistance was given by UNPROFOR, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Without the assistance of UNPROFOR he could not have been sent to Tuzla. He could have been arrested and detained in -- on the premises of the prison in the court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, I'll remind you of the first part of my question. It's correct, if you know this of course, that when processing this case, that is finding writing paper, cameras and so on, all this was provided by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other cases, such help was not provided, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all other cases, as far as the court is concerned, we had no help from the UN, the UN civilian police in Srebrenica. Sometimes they may have given such assistance to the public security station but I don't know that. I'm not aware of it. I would just like to add that in early 1995, the UN civilian police started visiting the court and inquiring about the cases we were dealing with and asking if we needed assistance, and then who gave us typing paper and also made it possible for us to interview a person who was a victim/witness and the murderer had been arrested and he was in Tuzla, because he had run away from the Srebrenica free zone, he was arrested in Tuzla, and then with the help of UNPROFOR we went to the village where this girl who had been wounded lived and took a statement from her. So those were the instances of assistance we received. The moment we received such assistance, it was easier for us to do our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. A special problem for you was the problem of defenders, was it not -- of Defence counsel, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, you had no attorneys and none of the lawyers there wanted to act as Defence counsel, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all living in a very small area, two kilometres long, and we saw each other every day. Those who were lawyers were afraid for their lives. They did not want to act in cases of people who were murderers and so on, and according to our law on criminal procedure, the court must have a list of attorneys who can be appointed if the accused does not have Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you the following about this. There was no way you could take any measures against a lawyer who refused to act as Defence counsel. There was no way you could punish him?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You delivered to Tuzla several pieces of information and several letters drawing attention to this problem, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I felt that the job we were doing was a highly responsible one, that it was regulated by law, and nothing should be done in proceedings against an accused that was contrary to the law. I tried to ensure legality to the best of my ability. I sent letters to the Court in Tuzla and to the ministry in Sarajevo, drawing their attention to our problems, the fact that we didn't have the legislation, that we didn't have Defence counsel, and so on. And we could not complete a single trial because of all these problems. And then we would have to do things again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness another document? This is an excerpt from the law on criminal procedure, Article 67, prescribing the conditions for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, while you are waiting for this document, to save time I will quote. "If there are not enough attorneys at law in the seat of the court, the president of the court shall, at the request of the accused person or a person under paragraph 3 herein, permit the appointment of a law graduate who is capable of providing the accused with help in his defence." In this connection, I will ask you the following, Mr. Mr. Omerovic: It's correct, is it not, that this law on criminal procedure was adopted as republican law of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by a decree law enacted by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this became the law of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So only a lawyer, a law graduate or, rather -- no, only an attorney --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only an attorney at law could be a Defence counsel but if an attorney at law wasn't available, it could be a law graduate. You never received any information that this provision had been amended to say that someone who was not a law graduate could act as Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never received any such provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever hear after this -- did you ever know that somebody who was not a graduate -- a law graduate defend -- act as defence council for anyone in legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of this. This seems abnormal to me because a person who is not a law graduate, who doesn't have the expert knowledge or qualifications, how can such a person provide legal assistance to an accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document will become Defence Exhibit D289.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, you were unable to overcome the issue of the two phases or two instances within the same proceedings provided a person in detention in Srebrenica appealed against a decision because it had to be forwarded to the court in Tuzla or to Sarajevo in case the Supreme Court had to decide about the issue?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We had to forward the complete file, together with the appeal, and we had no such ability.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to that, you had the problem of not being -- not having subject-matter jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And I demanded an explanation in order to solve that problem in all of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Akagic, who was the district Prosecutor tried to bridge such gap by trying to define competence in her documents?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1994, by the Ministry of Justice decision, the basic Prosecutor's office in Srebrenica received competences that usually belonged to the Prosecutor's office of higher instance in Tuzla and the basic court in Tuzla -- in Srebrenica never expanded its competence in relation to the instances of higher military courts?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, and there is a logical explanation. In order to try against the most serious offences and where sentences include significant number of imprisonment, the ministry decided that such competences should not be left to the basic court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor in Srebrenica was able to undertake certain measures that fell within the competence of the district military prosecutor's office, provided they reported the prosecutor in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The transfer of competences from Tuzla to the basic court in Srebrenica never happened, with the exception of the urgent measures that had to be taken and that only happened on the 6th of February 1995?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was quite persistent and I kept demanding that, and then we received a document from the president of the district military court authorising us to deal with some of the issues that fell under the competence of the court in Tuzla. Therefore, we could undertake measures including urgent issues, for example, securing traces, exhibits, and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, this did not include conducting investigations for earlier offences but only those that happened at that very time?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The urgent measures at the moment an offence happened, so just the current situations or incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon the prosecutor's request, the basic court in Srebrenica did conduct investigations that fell under the competence of the district military court for the contemporaneous offences?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then it forwarded those cases to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a clarification. There is a part of my question missing in the transcript. I asked the

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: were forwarded to Tuzla, these were criminal offences that took place at that time. This did not include some earlier offences, or offences from earlier periods."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your question. We only dealt with the offences that occurred at the time when the court was formed, and during the time when a prosecutor would submit a request for criminal investigation and would submit the report. And then we acted on their request.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Practically speaking, neither the Prosecutor in Srebrenica nor you who were employed with the Court could not legally deal with the cases that fell under the competence of the district military court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct and we were fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the contributing factor was the slow process on the decisions on custody and the forwarding of persons and the cases that --

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were objective circumstances. The process was slow. We were unable to forward the documents. We didn't know when the other side would receive it, perhaps a couple of months later, and later on I was even doubtful of whether they received them ever in Tuzla because we had no communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon the proposal of the military prosecutor in Tuzla, you would issue a decision on custody for the perpetrator of a particular offence because otherwise you could not detain him?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not really competent to issue such a decision?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it did not fall under the competences of our court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you used the packet radio to forward the material received from Srebrenica to the district military court in Tuzla and then waited for months for the decision of the district military court in Tuzla, and by law you had to serve that decision within 48 hours on the accused?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, we had a case of triple homicide. Should we release that person in a very limited area such as Srebrenica, any other work done by the court would be senseless. We knew we had no competence but we interpreted the provisions on criminal procedure rather openly and liberally, and we did so in order to prevent further escalation of crime in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But when you issued decisions via this procedure, it meant serious problems for you because the opinion was formed that the court acted illegally and was trying to pass its own laws?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I wanted to clarify. When we began working as the basic court and the prosecutor's office, our impression was that all citizens of Srebrenica were civilians because the demilitarisation had occurred before that, but once we would conduct an investigation and decide on detention, a part of those people were returned to the lists of soldiers, so then we had the issue of whether a particular person was a civilian or a soldier. In essence, he was just a regular citizen but he was on the list of soldiers and we were not competent to try, and that was something that occurred a couple of months after we started working.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You notified about that the district military court in Tuzla, and you stressed that that was the impression not only with the population of Srebrenica but with some people who held certain positions there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was illegal work, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Having in mind the laws that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, we did act illegally, but from a different standpoint, given the situation in a besieged city in which we had to deal with the problems, this was something we had to do. For example, you have a house burning and you are not a fireman but you do try to salvage what you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you had best intentions in mind, including the authorities in Srebrenica, but nonetheless, you were exposed to certain pressure in order to release some of the detained?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You reported this to the people that you thought were the command of the 8th Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put a document before the witness. This is a document from the command of the 8th operations group dated the 22nd of February 1995, signed by Nedzad Bektic. I would kindly ask the witness to take a look at the document. The title is "Urgent Submission of Documents." I will quote the document. It is rather short. It states the following: "In view of the fact that the Srebrenica enclave is completely cut off from the rest of the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that there is no military court in the area," first of all, before I continue, would you agree that this document was sent to the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Therefore, they demanded or requested that they urgently submit decisions regarding the following cases, and the names follow. Since there has been mounting pressure on the representatives of the lower court in Srebrenica, particularly from the commander of the independent mountain battalion, senior captain Ejub Golic who even made threats involving physical violence and in view of the fact that the deadlines for detention pursuant to the law on criminal procedure have expired, we once again request urgent submission of the aforementioned decisions since the persons in question are still in detention." In relation to that, Mr. Omerovic, I wanted to ask the following: This document shows, does it not, that the assistant commander for security, as they called him, Mr. Nedzad Bektic from the 8th operational group Srebrenica, reacted receiving received your warning, and informed the 2nd Corps in Tuzla about the issue?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. I spoke with Mr. Nedzad Bektic. We all knew each other in Srebrenica because this was a very limited area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bektic therefore did know about the threats made to Mr. Ejub Golic and he notified the 2nd Corps about that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is clear from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you are familiar with that as well?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we assign a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this will become Defence Exhibit D290. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, you sent several letters such as the one from the 23rd of February 1995 that I showed you just a while ago, and you notified the district military court in Tuzla that you will not take action in case that is fall under the competence of that court in Tuzla because of the reasons we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I told them that we will not take any action because we found ourselves in a very poor situation, and I thought that I could be even held criminally liable for abuse of power or illegal implementation of laws once peace is back in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask the usher to show the witness another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a lower court in Srebrenica document, number SU 19/95 dated 1st April 1995. Witness, could you please take a look at the document? I will quote the last paragraph on the first page as well as the first paragraph on the second page. It states -- but before I begin, this is a document signed or, rather, with your name at the end. Would you agree with me, did you make this document?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, can we have the second page also on the ELMO, please? All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I am seeing this document since 1995. Some of the documents I did see with the Prosecutor before that, but I needed to refresh my memory on this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that you created this document?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now quote a part of the document. "We are surprised that in the documents we received from your court [the rulings ordering investigation, the ruling ordering detention, and the letter rogatory] there is no mention of our rulings on detention [although they have been forwarded to you]. Not even a negative context [if you believed them to be contrary to the law]. Are we to understand that the district military court in Tuzla has not received our rulings on detention [in these particular cases], or does it mean that your court assumes that the accused [in specific cases] remained in custody according to our rulings for only three days, and that they were free at the time your court passed a ruling on detention? We now have a situation in which several individuals have been detained for three or four months, having received from the competent district military court only one ruling on detention [for 30 days] according to which the detention period shall be reckoned from the moment of arrest. Due to that, we must admit that the pressure being exerted on this Court is justified. However, this Court has no basis in law to either suspend or rule to extend detention. This has put us in a difficult and unenviable position vis-a-vis these particular cases." A brief question on this, Mr. Omerovic. The fact you listed and the facts I quoted, are they correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to deal with the problems but given the circumstances of the siege and the inability to communicate, nothing much could be done. But these facts are true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please assign a number to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become Defence Exhibit D291.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put D214 before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the district military court in Tuzla and signed by the president of that court, Mr. Ismet Trumic. Please look at the document. I will quote part of the document to you, starting with the third sentence in the first paragraph: "It is evident that due to objective and in good measure subjective missions by the participants in the proceedings, the -- there is -- or, rather, your court and the district military court and vice versa, there have been some serious delays and our correspondence, decisions, and other documents are reaching you with a one- or two-month delay. The situation is similar with a delivery of your documents to us. This is one of the reasons why your decisions on detentions and criminal reports are received with a delay of as many as three months after the incident itself which means that this period cannot legally be covered by the decision of this Court. In fact, this court cannot adopt a single decision before it has formally received a request to investigate or an indictment for a case. It is clear that the matter of solving cases that concern persons in Srebrenica and that come under the jurisdiction of the district military court cannot be resolved satisfactorily despite the efforts by the lower court in Srebrenica and the district military court in Tuzla." First of all, in connection with this, I will ask you the following, Mr. Omerovic. Do you agree that Mr. Trumic, Mr. Ismet Trumic, the president of the district court, sent you this letter in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received this letter in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document confirms that the district court in Tuzla neither wanted nor was able to issue any decision retroactively covering your decisions on custody whereby people were kept in detention in Srebrenica for months?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The competent court can act only after it has received a motion and the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And therefore, you had to declare yourself not having subject matter jurisdiction, and hand over such cases by packet communications, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time, this was the -- our salvation. We could declare ourselves not competent, not having subject matter competence, otherwise we would have been breaking the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness another document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, please look at this document. This is a judgement of the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 402/02 of the 17th of April 2002. Mr. Omerovic, I will read to you what it says. "The appeal filed by the deputy cantonal Prosecutor in Tuzla is hereby rejected as unfounded and the verdict of the cantonal court in Tuzla number K110/96 dated on June 28th, 2002 is hereby confirmed." Underneath this it says "justification or statement of reasons," and it is evident that the verdict quoted of the cantonal court in Tuzla acquitted the accused of having committed the crime of murder from Article 36, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Omerovic, Ferid Mehmedovic is one of the accused whose case in 1994 you forwarded from Srebrenica to the district military court in Tuzla and this is the case which was shown to you in great detail yesterday by the Prosecutor who went through a number of documents with you. Is this that person?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same person and the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please look at page 3 of this document, paragraph 2, and I will quote the relevant parts to you. It can be seen -- the relevant part of the decision of the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it can be seen from the case file that "statements of the defendant and witnesses in their preliminary proceedings before the basic court in Srebrenica were submitted to the district court in Tuzla on September the 13th 1994 by a teleprinter and that the questioned persons, the investigative judge and the records-taker did not sign the statements. It also arises from the file that original minutes from questioning of the defendant and hearing of the witnesses in the investigation were not found. The defendant Ferid Mehmedovic and witnesses Amir Hogic [phoen] and Fadil Music who were requested at the main hearing, having been presented -- having presented their statements arising from a telegram sent from the basic court in Srebrenica to the district court in Tuzla stated that they had been questioned at the basic court in Srebrenica but that the statements they had given on that occasion were not identical to the statements that were submitted by teleprinter and presented to them." Mr. Omerovic, I will ask you the following about this. The minutes of witness interviews, as well as statements by the accused, were typed out and delivered by packet communications or by teleprinter to Tuzla. This is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I can clarify. When interviewing a defendant and witnesses, all the persons present, the investigating judge, the witness, and the court clerk, sign the minutes, and they have to do this. However, we were unable to forward the originals of these documents to Tuzla. All we could do was retype the text, only such a retyped text could be delivered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will ask you the following about this: In order to be used in court proceedings, they had to be signed by the judge, the court clerk, the accused, or the witness, whoever was being interviewed, and they had to bear the stamp of the court, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Otherwise, they would have no legal validity as evidence in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unsigned and unstamped, they could not be used at all in legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am surprised that the court dealing with this was able, on the basis of such evidence and such minutes, to hand down a judgement, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, maybe I have not shown this to you but would you please look at the first sentence? The Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina acquitted the accused. Would you have a look and tell me if you agree with what I've just said? Look at the first sentence of the statement of reasons in this judgement. It says, "Pursuant to a judgement of the cantonal court in Tuzla, pursuant to Article 345, item 3 of the law on criminal proceedings, the cantonal court in Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see now. I see now. This is an appeal by the Prosecutor because he was acquitted by the court of first instance. And this is quite proper because in view of the kind of evidence that we had, this had to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will ask you the following. If the district military prosecutor received such unsigned statements, he could not rely on such statements as evidence, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The persons who worked on this communications system, when they were retyping the text, they could make a mistake, whether intentionally or not. They could fail to type out the entire original text. We had no way of checking this. So these unsigned minutes were not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Omerovic, during your testimony yesterday, you were shown six cases falling within the competence of the court in Tuzla which had been forwarded to them by packet communication. If I tell you -- if I put it to you that apart from the case of Ferid Mehmedovic which I have shown you and which has been completed with an acquittal on appeal, no sentence has been passed even after all these years, would you be surprised to hear this?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In view of the gravity of these crimes and the evidence required, I think there is no way for the trial to be conducted properly and for a sentence to be handed -- for a conviction to be handed down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these be given exhibit numbers, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will receive number -- Defence Exhibit D292.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, I will ask you some more questions about this topic. The district Prosecutor and the district military court in Tuzla were aware that cases falling within their competence in the Srebrenica area could not be dealt with, and that is why they asked the competent state organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina to establish a department of the military court in Srebrenica, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They were aware of the problems and on their part, they wanted to solve this problem by establishing a department of the court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness another document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the transitional municipal mayor of Srebrenica municipality, Mr. Fahrudin Salihovic and it's dated the 24th of March, 1995. It is unsigned but would you please look at the document? And it is addressed to the district military court in Tuzla. As the document is not long, I will quote it in full. It says here, "the Tuzla district military court, and the Tuzla district military prosecutor's office in their letters numbers SU 20/95 of the 16th of January 1995, and number A-11/95 of the 16th of January 1995, requested that we forward the names of persons holing a degree in law so that they can be appointed to the posts of judges and deputy military prosecutor in the Srebrenica department of the military court and the prosecutor's office. Since we received your letters, we have tried in every way to ensure these persons and to find a way to get the Srebrenica department started. Unfortunately, despite our efforts, we are unable to find adequately qualified persons because there are none in the free territory of Srebrenica municipality. We are aware of the situation and the need to establish such a department in Srebrenica, but we cannot set it up for now. "If you are willing to assist us in this matter, please help us in any way you can. In our view, however, it would be best if our graduate lawyers, who are in Tuzla, could be transferred to Srebrenica. We think that this is the only possible solution at the moment." Mr. Omerovic, in connection with this, I will ask you the following: The correspondence about the establishment of a department of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Tuzla district military court was carried on between the War Presidency of Srebrenica and the Tuzla district military court. It fell within their competence, and this can be seen here, can it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The transitional municipal council had already been set up as the local parliament, and a transitional mayor had been elected as the executive organ of this legislative organ. At the point in time when this document was sent, it was compiled by the transitional mayor and addressed to the district military court, and it concerned the establishment of a department of the military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. I thought that it was actually the transitional council that succeeded the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the correspondence concerning the establishment of this court, it was the civilian authorities that had the competence to engage in this correspondence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, and today, you told us that among the populations of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and the surrounding villages that remained in Srebrenica throughout the war, there were only a few lawyers, including you. The only lawyer in the whole command of the 8th Operative Group was Avdo Majstorovic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was assigned there in early 1995 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Early 935?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may be wrong but he was the only law graduate in the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before that, Avdo Majstorovic was not in Srebrenica. He was from Bratunac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo Majstorovic was from Bratunac municipality. That's where he worked. And during the war, he lived in Konjevic Polje and that's where he was on the free territory of Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was there that he performed some sort of duty trying to organise a local government, as far as was possible?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He and another graduate lawyer from Bratunac, Dzemail Becirevic. The two of them tried to organise something over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dzemail Becirevic was in fact the president of the War Presidency of Bratunac, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. He performed the duty of president of the War Presidency of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now go back. I won't show the document in order not to waste time, but you remember that today the Prosecutor showed you a document signed by Amir Mehmedovic. Does the nickname Gera mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know who this is about. I know him by his nickname because, as I said, when the Prosecutor asked me, I said I couldn't remember him by his name but you could recall some people by their nicknames. I know who this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Amir Mehmedovic at the time was in his second year of law school? That's where he was when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was certainly not a graduate lawyer, because I knew all of them personally. I didn't know he was the second year student of the law school but I did know for certain that he did not graduate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic are you ready --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document, the one that has been made use of last, being a letter allegedly sent by Fahrudin Salihovic mayor of the municipality of Srebrenica, it's being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D293.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document, I wanted to ask you the following: It is correct, is it not, that the War Presidency of Srebrenica, at the time, had a real problem. Avdo Majstorovic, Becirevic Dzemail, Esad Nukic, these were the people that were a part of the transitional council and the problem was to find the personnel, people adequate for the council?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yesterday I was shown a document by the Prosecutor. I recognised it. That was a reply of the president of the district military court to the transitional municipal prefect, and he said that there were five lawyers in the area of Srebrenica. He listed the five of them, and yesterday I mentioned that they were all tasked with their functions. They occupied positions where there had to have been lawyers, and had they left the positions in the court or in the other bodies were -- would have been left empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their request for the transfer of Srebrenica lawyers to be appointed to the department of the Prosecutor's office of the Court in Tuzla was fully justified?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree we did not have sufficient number of people to cover all of our needs. It suffices to say that within the police station there was not a single lawyer, and in organisational terms there had to have been at least two or three.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A question on a different topic. It is correct, is it not, that formally and legally speaking, Srebrenica was under the competence of the prosecutor's office in Tuzla, as well as the district military court, but only in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In real terms, it was not. We saw here that the court in Tuzla and the prosecutor's office in Tuzla did not have real authority in the territory of Srebrenica because of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, in Srebrenica, itself, there were no military organs that would be capable to detect evidence and perpetrators of criminal offences that fell under the competence of the district military court?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, neither such an organ nor an individual existed there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, to clarify a detail, when you were speaking about the police station and when you said that there were no lawyers, you had in mind the station in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The public security station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are familiar with the fact that there was a decree law during the war about district military courts and in relation to that I wanted to ask the following: First of all, are you familiar with such a decree law?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That particular decree on district military courts is something you did not receive at least until May 1993, if ever at all during the war in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Not a single provision or regulation or a decree, we did not receive any of that up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you ever receive such a decree during the war?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether it was a part of the group of the regulation which we received from Sarajevo when we received the collection of laws put into force until that moment. But as I stated then, and as I reported to the court in Tuzla, the collection was incomplete. So I cannot say anything with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But what you can say with certainty is that you did not receive that decree until the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certain. We did not receive any regulation until the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, there was no investigating judge to whom an arrested person could be turned over, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no such a judicial organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nor an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until that time, until the demilitarisation, it was not possible to take a detained person to see the closest and competent prosecutor or judge, which was -- who was in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation, practically speaking, neither the military police nor military security or any military officer in Srebrenica had no authority to conduct any investigative task, including detaining or arresting anyone?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only competence was that in possession of the public security station in Srebrenica. That is the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that's because Srebrenica was demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will kindly ask the usher to put another document before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 14/94. Could you please take a look at it? There is a decision on the election of the War Presidencies of the assemblies of the municipalities of Srebrenica, Kalinovik and Kupres of the 22nd of June 1994. You mentioned that you attended the sessions of the War Presidency. Could you please take a look at the names listed, or, rather, please take a look at the part referring to the municipality of Srebrenica, under 1, it states, "The War Presidency of the municipal assembly of Srebrenica, questioned and the names are Fahrudin Salihovic as president of the Presidency; Hamdija Fejzic, president of the executive committee of the municipality; Suljo Hasanovic, chief of the department of the Ministry of Defence; Hakija Meholjic, as chief of the public security station; Hajrudin Avdic as president of the SDA of the assemblymen's club, and item 6, Murat Efendic. Do you agree that the name of Naser Oric is not one of the names?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. This was the period of the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you believe the reason for that was the fact that Srebrenica was demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to add something. The sixth name on the list, that of Murat Efendic. That's a person who was not in Srebrenica but in Sarajevo, so the five people on the list comprised the War Presidency and the sixth member was in Srebrenica -- in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So a military representative in Srebrenica could not have been a member of the civilian body?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was invited to attend the sessions when there was a need for that, the same as you were invited should the war president find it necessary -- the War Presidency find it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember perhaps three occasions when we discussed security issues, issues pertaining to public order, and the establishing of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could kind kindly ask that this excerpt from the Official Gazette be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I just wanted to direct your attention to something. On the same page, where there is the mention of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, there are two lawyers that we mentioned previously, Sinanovic Resid, who was the second of the Presidency, as well as Avdo Majstorovic who was the president of the executive committee. Those two people that we mentioned earlier were appointed to the War Presidency of the municipal assembly of Bratunac municipality, and they were in Srebrenica, and these were their functions at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, this document will become Defence Exhibit D294.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some meetings and the prosecutor asked you about some of the sessions that you attended, and you specifically mentioned two sessions of the War Presidency during -- or rather when you gave your statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were giving that statement, if need be, we can refresh your memory but I believe you mentioned some of that today as well. You said that on one occasion, Naser Oric, in May or June 1994, attended a session of the War Presidency, and then he appeared again in April 1995 once. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the occasion that occurred in 1995. He did attend the meeting. That was immediately prior to him leaving the enclave, and we had certain problems concerning the assault on the prison by Ejub Golic when he was trying to release his friend from prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask questions of you about that.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the meeting when Naser Oric was definitely present, and I believe there was another instance when we discussed the issues of law and order, but it is rather difficult to remember after so many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you remember well at least one such meeting where issues of offences as well as detention of the members of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were discussed?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As pertains to Mr. Naser Oric, his view at that time, as in any other time, but you do remember that one situation, so I'm asking you only about that, his view at the time was that he supported both the police and the Court in their attempts to establish order in Srebrenica, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Naser Oric never tried to intervene with the work of the court. I can confirm that, and he even supported us asking that we be persistent in the establishing law and order, and there are the meetings of the sessions in 1995. When we had those significant problems pertaining to law and order, he attended a session and he supported our work, and offered his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Omerovic, that was precisely the reason why Emir Halilovic, in your presence, threatened to him to kill him. You saw Emir Halilovic threatening Oric to kill him, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen from the documents. That was on the day when he saw two Serbs, a mother and a son, and the day when he injured Adil Muhic. On that day he came in front of the building. I was in my apartment and I heard someone shouting and cursing in front of the building. I came out on to the balcony and I saw a young lad I didn't know until then. He had a gun in his hand. He was waving it around and he looked drunk and crazed, and he was shouting something along the lines of Naser, come out, he cursed his mother and he was threatening to kill him, and I just went into the building because he could incidentally shoot and a stray bullet could hit the building, and tomorrow I found out that he caused grave injury to Adil Muhic. He hit him with the handle of his gun and he put the gun in his mouth. I even found out that he stopped some other people and mistreated them the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I'm about to move to a larger document, perhaps this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. How much more time do you have, roughly, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 20 to 25 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break then. We'll have a break of 25 minutes starting from now, which means five past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic and Ms. Richardson in particular, please listen to what I have to say. Something urgent and important has arisen which requires my presence elsewhere and which I cannot avoid. I mean, there is no way I can avoid it. I have managed to prolong it until 6.35 which is 20 -- 25 minutes from now. If I could, I ask you to try and cut down as much as you can and you eventually to limit your re-examination in a way to make sure that I am out of this courtroom by 6.35, because I have to rush elsewhere. It's not something over which I have control. I'm just needed elsewhere. And these things happen. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We on our part --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. Would the usher please show the witness another document, the last document we shall show the witness this evening?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the transitional municipal council of Srebrenica dated the 11th of March 1995. Witness, please look at the document. As we are short of time, witness, would you right away look at the third paragraph of the document? I will quote it to you. "After an analysis of several hours, we have all unanimously concluded that the political and security situation in the enclave is very difficult due to a number of factors. And one of the factors leading to the deterioration of the situation is the incidents caused by Ejub Ganic and in order to overcome this situation, a number of conclusions have been made, including the following. Full support was given to our commander of the 28th division, Brigadier Naser Oric. A decision was adopted to arrest and bring into custody at the municipal prison Nezir Merdzic and Sadik Begic, which has already been done," and so on. Mr. Omerovic, you attended this meeting where Mr. Oric was present. It's correct, is it not, that on that occasion, Oric gave his absolute support to the standpoint that Golic should be transferred to Tuzla and there handed over to the relevant authorities. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was aware that he would thus be causing dissatisfaction and division in a part of what remained as the armed forces and this was discussed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also discussed. The taking of Ejub Golic to Tuzla was discussed because Naser had to do this personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So Naser had to do it personally and that is why the decision was made at this meeting that he, as the commander, should be given full support, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Golic, together with Oric, was transferred to Tuzla by helicopter and there he was handed over to the corps and the appropriate authorities, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was transferred to Tuzla by helicopter so that he could be tried there and proceedings initiated against him and so that he could be handed over to the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this document be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D295.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will put only a few more very brief questions to you. Today you were asked by the Prosecutor about Naser Oric's physical appearance. What you recall with certainty is that Naser Oric had a beard?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naser Oric had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot assert that you ever saw him clean-shaven. Did I understand you correctly? Not at any time -- I apologise, I'm referring only to the period of the war. So during the war period, from July 1992 until he left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert this with certainty. I think that in this latter period before he left Srebrenica, he didn't always have a beard, but I can't be 100 per cent sure. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you allow for this possibility that, in the latter period, just before he left Srebrenica. But up to the demilitarisation in 1992 and 1993, do you remember ever seeing him without a beard?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have cut short my questions. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We really appreciate that. And I knew I could count on your cooperation before I entered the courtroom, and I anticipate now that Ms. Richardson would not take advantage of the lot of time that remains to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, you testified previously that you are from Bratunac. You're not originally from Srebrenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Srebrenica, but I lived my whole life in Bratunac. My family moved to Bratunac when I was 40 days old and I lived in Bratunac until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You weren't familiar with all of the individuals in Srebrenica when you returned in July of 1992 to 1993? You didn't know everyone?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to the document that I showed you yesterday where it listed military police and you indicated that you knew at least three of them, you didn't know the others, correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them. At least not by name. I couldn't recognise the names of the others. I did know these three because later on, they were members of the civilian police, and they often came to the court to bring us criminal reports or bring in suspects. So later on, they were civilian policemen and that's how I got to know them. I didn't know them while they were in the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for taking up time but I don't see how this question follows from the cross-examination. I did not deal with this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, it doesn't follow and it's a question that was asked or was relied to by the witness already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish base on the cross-examination of Madam Vidovic that -- in fact that there were no professional policemen in Srebrenica at the time so that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In addition to the three individuals, you stated that you knew Dzanan Dzananovic and you worked with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mispronounced the last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise. If you're familiar with that individual could you just tell us the name?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall -- could you just jog my memory or read it again? I don't --.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will try my best to pronounce it correctly. Dzanan Dzananovic. He's the individual that's listed on P507 and he was involved in the investigation, the criminal report for Emir Halilovic, and it's spelled, perhaps this will help, D-Z-A-N-A-N, D-Z-A-N-A-N-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzananovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You're familiar with that individual?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with his work as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked quite correctly and professionally as a policeman while he was in the civilian police. That's when I knew him, after the demilitarisation. I did not know him before the demilitarisation so I cannot say anything about his previous work. Later on, he was responsible and professional worker.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend any of the military police meetings?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And yesterday I also showed you a page of that same document where it was indicated that a theft had occurred. Were you involved in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that what you showed me was an official note by a military policeman saying that there had been a theft - this was in 1992 - and that the police had discovered the perpetrator. There were no criminal proceedings against this person, nor was a criminal report later filed with the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you're not aware during that period of time, or you were not involved with any investigations by the military police, correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday was the first time I had seen that document. It was a handwritten official note which somebody jotted down in 1992, probably working in the military police. I had never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now with respect to the actions that you testified to, you were not in the military, were you, Mr. Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- at the outset, in the village, I had gone to, a village guard was organised and then, together with all the other men, I stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm referring only to Srebrenica, nothing more. Were you -- did you attend any meeting involving the planning of actions in Srebrenica where the military was present? Or I should say members of the military?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend any meeting where any actions were planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you testified that you went to look for food, did any of the combatants prevent you from taking food or anything else on that day?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a long column of civilians. I set out on my own. Nobody told me to go. I had no food for myself and my family, and I went on my own initiative together with some other persons from the building in which I resided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, if you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to get Mr. Omerovic to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour this witness hasn't said that in the -- on that occasion that he took any food. So the notion that he should have -- that someone should have prevented him from taking something which he never took is an erroneous assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that he took. That's what I understood, that he went there because he had to, he had to feed his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was a separate occasion but he hasn't testified that he actually took anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I figured out. Anyway, he can clarify that. And please, the question is, the substance of the question is the following: In this quest for food that you undertook joining the others, were you ever stopped or impeded by the fighters, by the combatants, from taking food? This is the question that you need to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never even reached the place where the food was. I turned back four or five kilometres before that place because the bombing and shelling had started and I was afraid, in fear of my life, so I went back. I didn't take anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, I'll move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were asked on cross-examination and shown a document, P48, where there was an indication of a summary court martial instituted in Srebrenica. My question is respect to this court. Did you attend all of the War Presidency meetings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already told us, he attended at most three.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well my follow-up question then to the witness -- maybe it's an obvious one and I won't ask it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this same document, were you involved in any issues related to Serb prisoners, any crimes committed against them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked this question earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a follow-up from the document that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What you asked him is whether he received any reports, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So this question is whether he was involved in any of the issues related to Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already explained this as best I could in my testimony so far. At that session of the War Presidency to which I was invited for the establishment of a military court martial, this decision was not even made. It was someone's erroneous interpretation. This was an extended session. No such decision had been prepared and, looking at the minutes, it is certain that no decision was made to establish a military court martial. It was never established, it never operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, I'm not referring to the meeting you attended. I think you testified about that sufficiently. But my question to you is: Did you attend other meetings?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained all the meetings I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish -- he's answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on to the next question. I don't believe the witness answered about whether or not he was involved in any issues related to the Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he told us already that he has answered that question. And he said what he had -- all that he had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You testified as well about an incident involving Emir Halilovic where he was threatening Naser Oric. If you could just answer request a yes or no because I am out of time. Could you tell me if you're aware if Naser Oric was in the building at the time that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that point in time, Naser was in the building, in his flat, but I didn't see him from the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you see him go into the building?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's that's -- that was high question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. We don't have any further questions for you, Mr. Omerovic. I wish to thank you, first of all, Madam Vidovic and Ms. Richardson for being practical and enabling us to finish now. Basically this means that you are free to go back to your country. On behalf of my two colleagues, Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, I should like to thank you, sir, for coming over and giving testimony in this case. You'll receive all the assistance that's necessary to facilitate your journey back home and on behalf of everyone present here I should like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am glad if I have managed to explain the situation to you and the way we worked, and if I have been of assistance in your difficult decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you up been. Thank you. Tomorrow we will have the next witness starting at 2.15, I think in this same courtroom, and then there is going to be a meeting which you are aware of on Tuesday during the second break in my Chamber, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the Prosecution had an announcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I thank you Defence counsel, not for reminding me. I didn't know whether to pre-empt the five minutes or else -- since we have informed the Defence counsel that the Prosecution will not be calling the witness Sanarac that's scheduled next week for the first and the second. I did want to make the Trial Chamber aware that we've already conveyed the information to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I prefer to concentrate on this tomorrow because now I have switched over --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's what I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- switched over to the other matter that I have to attend to and I wouldn't like to switch back to this now. We'll deal with it tomorrow. Thank you.
